turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. ____. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Doctor. Nice to meet you. Well, I guess... the main reason I’m here is, well, it's work stuff mostly. I'm a medical services manager, so I oversee a few different outpatient clinics, which means I'm usually juggling a lot of moving parts—staffing, vendors, patient flow, facility maintenance, all of that. And I'm actually really good when I'm on my feet and dealing with people, but... the thing is, anything that takes real, sitting-down brain work, I just... it feels like I hit a wall. A literal brick wall. 

Like, I have to do these monthly budget and compliance reports, or sometimes I'm in charge of planning a big multi-site health event, which is a huge deal for our network. And I know it matters. I know exactly how important it is for the funding and the upper management. But the second I sit down at my desk to actually look at the spreadsheets or draft the event proposals, I just can't do it. I keep putting it off and putting it off. I'll go check the supply rooms, I'll chat with the front desk staff, I'll find a dozen other little fires to put out just to avoid sitting there and doing the heavy thinking. 

And it's not that I don't understand the work—I have my degree, I've been in healthcare administration for years, I know what needs to be done—but the mental block is just so intense. I'll stare at the screen and feel this overwhelming urge to get up. It just builds up until I'm incredibly stressed about the deadlines, and I'm taking the stress home with me, and honestly I'm just so tired of fighting myself every time I need to sit down and focus on a complex task.

symptom_reasoning.S006: The patient explicitly states they avoid and put off tasks requiring 'sitting-down brain work' or 'heavy thinking' like budget reports and event proposals.

turns.doctor_question: Did you have similar trouble focusing, following through, or getting organized as a child?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, wow, yes. Absolutely. You know, it's funny you ask that because I was actually just thinking about this the other day, just reflecting on how long this has been a pattern in my life. If you go all the way back to, gosh, elementary school—I went to this great little school, really dedicated teachers—but every single parent-teacher conference, it was the exact same story. I mean, literally every year, like a broken record. 

The teachers would sit down with my parents and they'd always start with a compliment, right? They'd say, "He's such a bright boy, he really is, he grasps the concepts so quickly"—but then the other shoe would drop. They told my parents I was just always daydreaming. I'd be staring out the window, completely lost in my own world, watching the cars go by or just off in space while everyone else was doing their math or reading. 

And the organization... oh man, it was a complete disaster. My desk at school was like a black hole. I was constantly losing worksheets. Sometimes I'd even do the work, but then the paper would just get crumpled up in the back of my desk or shoved into a random textbook, and I'd completely forget to turn it in. It actually got so bad that my mother had to step in and basically become my project manager. Every single night, without fail, she would make me stand there in the kitchen while she physically opened my backpack and went through it. She had to check every folder, pull out the wrinkled assignments, and make sure I actually packed my finished homework. Because if she didn't check that backpack every single night, I just wouldn't turn anything in. I'd go to school with all the right intentions, but it would just vanish from my brain the second I walked into the classroom. It was exhausting for her, I know it was, and honestly, looking back, I feel kind of guilty about how much extra work I caused her, but I just... I couldn't seem to keep it all straight on my own, even back then.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes being unable to sustain attention during class, stating they were always daydreaming and lost in their own world while others did math or reading.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient confirms failing to follow through on schoolwork, noting they would frequently forget to turn in assignments unless their mother intervened.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states their organization was a 'complete disaster' and describes their school desk as a 'black hole'.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient reports constantly losing worksheets and having papers crumpled up in their desk.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient mentions being distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as watching cars go by out the window during class.
